Plenty of collections were digitized years ago as whole-bed images: four or five photos crammed into one big file, still waiting to be cut apart. FrontBack opens those files too. Drop one on the window, or hand it an entire folder and let it work through them one after another.

Open the scans

Drag images, or a whole folder, onto the window. The File menu does the same with Open Bed Scan… and Open Folder of Bed Scans… A folder arrives as one ordered queue.

Every print gets boxed

The same detector that reads the glass reads the file: each photo found, straightened, and named. Adjust a box or draw a missed one exactly as you would live.

Split & Next

One click cuts every photo out of the original full-resolution pixels, saves it upright and numbered, and loads the next scan in the queue. Then the next.

The speed is the point: for a large collection there is nothing to click between files. Split, and the next scan is already on screen with its photos boxed. Your originals are read-only, and the split photos are written into the output folder you choose, so nothing can overwrite the scans you started with. Naming, numbering, auto-orientation, and back-pairing all behave exactly as they do at the scanner: split a sheet of fronts, then split the sheet of backs, and each back is matched to its front and saved as _b beside it.

What is FrontBack Scanner?

FrontBack Scanner is free photo scanning software for macOS and Windows. It drives the flatbed scanner you already own, finds every print you lay on the glass, and saves each one as its own cropped, straightened, right-side-up, numbered file. Flip the pile over and scan again, and it pairs each photo’s back with its front automatically. It also stitches prints larger than the scanner bed, and splits photos out of whole-bed scan files you already have. There is no account, no upload, no watermark, and no photo limit: the whole app is free.

Is FrontBack Scanner really free?

Yes. Completely free, with no account, no watermarks, and no limits. It’s built by Timeline Scan; if you later want your scanned photos dated and organized automatically, that’s our paid service, but the scanning app itself is free forever. If it saves you hours and you’d like to say thanks, you can leave an optional tip: the app never asks.

Which Macs does FrontBack Scanner run on?

Any Mac running macOS 14 (Sonoma) or newer, both Apple silicon and Intel. The download is signed and notarized by Apple, so it opens without security warnings.

Does FrontBack Scanner run on Windows?

Yes. The Windows version does everything the Mac version does and runs on Windows 10 (version 1809) and Windows 11, 64-bit. It works with any scanner that has a Windows driver, through Windows Image Acquisition (WIA).

Which scanners work with FrontBack Scanner?

Any scanner your computer can see. On a Mac, Wi-Fi and network all-in-ones that support AirScan/eSCL work with no driver at all, and USB flatbeds work through their macOS Image Capture driver. On Windows, anything with a Windows (WIA) scanner driver works, which covers virtually every flatbed and all-in-one. The Epson Perfection V600, for example, works on both after installing Epson’s free driver.

How many photos can I scan at once?

As many as fit on the glass. Most flatbeds hold four to six standard prints per pass, and auto-detect separates each one into its own cropped, straightened, right-side-up file. A 400-photo shoebox becomes roughly a hundred passes instead of four hundred single scans: that’s the whole point. Our guide to scanning multiple photos at once walks through a full session.

How does front-and-back pairing work?

Scan the fronts, then flip each photo over where it lies and scan again. FrontBack matches each back to its front by position on the glass and saves it with a suffix of your choosing (_b by default), so scan_0001.jpg and scan_0001_b.jpg stay together forever. In back mode it even detects the handwriting area on otherwise blank photo backs, and you can rewire any pairing by hand.

Can it scan photos bigger than the scanner bed?

Yes. Oversized mode scans a big print (a panorama, an 11 × 14, a mounted album page) in overlapping passes: scan one section, slide the photo, scan the next. Each pass aligns to the last automatically, even laid back crooked or turned, and Finish & Save writes one seamless full-resolution photo. For an album page, Chop It Up then cuts each mounted photo into its own file.

Can it split up scans I already have?

Yes, and no scanner is needed for it. Open an image file (File ▸ Open Bed Scan…), drag images straight onto the window, or point the app at a whole folder of flatbed scans. FrontBack detects every print in the current image, and Split & Next writes each one out as its own cropped, straightened, upright, numbered file, then immediately loads the next scan in the queue: a folder of hundreds of old whole-bed scans is worked through one after another. Every crop is cut from the original full-resolution pixels, and your source files are only ever read, never modified or overwritten. See how it works.

What if a photo is sideways or upside down on the glass?

Lay photos any way they land. FrontBack Scanner checks each print’s orientation with an on-device neural network, 99.8% accurate in our benchmarks, and saves every file right-side up. The bed preview shows the corrected photo before you scan, and one click on the ↻ badge keeps the original orientation if you ever disagree.

Do my photos leave my computer?

No. FrontBack Scanner talks directly to your scanner and saves files to a folder you choose on your computer. There is no account, no upload, and no cloud processing.

What quality are the scans?

FrontBack scans one lossless pass at up to your scanner’s full optical resolution (6400 dpi on an Epson V600) and saves archival-quality JPEGs with the true DPI embedded, so photos open at their real physical size. Because the crop happens after a single fixed-exposure pass, a cropped photo is pixel-identical to scanning it alone.

What if a photo is sideways or upside down on the glass? Lay photos any way they land. FrontBack Scanner checks each print’s orientation with an on-device neural network, 99.8% accurate in our benchmarks, and saves every file right-side up. The bed preview shows the corrected photo before you scan, and one click on the ↻ badge keeps the original orientation if you ever disagree. Do my photos leave my computer? No. FrontBack Scanner talks directly to your scanner and saves files to a folder you choose on your computer. There is no account, no upload, and no cloud processing. What quality are the scans? FrontBack scans one lossless pass at up to your scanner’s full optical resolution (6400 dpi on an Epson V600) and saves archival-quality JPEGs with the true DPI embedded, so photos open at their real physical size. What is FrontBack Scanner?

FrontBack Scanner is free photo scanning software for macOS and Windows. Flip the pile over and scan again, and it pairs each photo’s back with its front automatically. There is no account, no upload, no watermark, and no photo limit: the whole app is free.

Is FrontBack Scanner really free?

是的。 Completely free, with no account, no watermarks, and no limits. If it saves you hours and you’d like to say thanks, you can leave an optional tip: the app never asks.

Which Macs does FrontBack Scanner run on?

Any Mac running macOS 14 (Sonoma) or newer, both Apple silicon and Intel. The download is signed and notarized by Apple, so it opens without security warnings.

Does FrontBack Scanner run on Windows?

是的。 The Windows version does everything the Mac version does and runs on Windows 10 (version 1809) and Windows 11, 64-bit. It works with any scanner that has a Windows driver, through Windows Image Acquisition (WIA).

Which scanners work with FrontBack Scanner?

Any scanner your computer can see. On a Mac, Wi-Fi and network all-in-ones that support AirScan/eSCL work with no driver at all, and USB flatbeds work through their macOS Image Capture driver. On Windows, anything with a Windows (WIA) scanner driver works, which covers virtually every flatbed and all-in-one. The Epson Perfection V600, for example, works on both after installing Epson’s free driver.

How many photos can I scan at once?

As many as fit on the glass. Most flatbeds hold four to six standard prints per pass, and auto-detect separates each one into its own cropped, straightened, right-side-up file. A 400-photo shoebox becomes roughly a hundred passes instead of four hundred single scans: that’s the whole point. Our guide to scanning multiple photos at once walks through a full session.

How does front-and-back pairing work?

Scan the fronts, then flip each photo over where it lies and scan again. FrontBack matches each back to its front by position on the glass and saves it with a suffix of your choosing (_b by default), so scan_0001.jpg and scan_0001_b.jpg stay together forever. Each pass aligns to the last automatically, even laid back crooked or turned, and Finish & Save writes one seamless full-resolution photo. Yes, and no scanner is needed for it. Open an image file (File ▸ Open Bed Scan…), drag images straight onto the window, or point the app at a whole folder of flatbed scans. FrontBack detects every print in the current image, and Split & Next writes each one out as its own cropped, straightened, upright, numbered file, then immediately loads the next scan in the queue: a folder of hundreds of old whole-bed scans is worked through one after another. Lay photos any way they land. FrontBack Scanner checks each print’s orientation with an on-device neural network, 99.8% accurate in our benchmarks, and saves every file right-side up. The bed preview shows the corrected photo before you scan, and one click on the ↻ badge keeps the original orientation if you ever disagree.

Do my photos leave my computer?

No. FrontBack Scanner talks directly to your scanner and saves files to a folder you choose on your computer. There is no account, no upload, and no cloud processing.

What quality are the scans?

FrontBack scans one lossless pass at up to your scanner’s full optical resolution (6400 dpi on an Epson V600) and saves archival-quality JPEGs with the true DPI embedded, so photos open at their real physical size.
